content: 1. Postpartum breastfeeding women using Norplant implants or progesterone vaginal rings do not experience changes in maternal bone turnover or bone density during lactation or after weaning. (Diaz et al., 1999) 2. A randomized controlled trial comparing progestin-only contraceptives to combined oral contraceptive pills found no significant adverse effects on lactation. (Espey et al., 2012) 3. Early postpartum use of contraceptive implants, such as Norplant, does not negatively impact lactogenesis, as demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial. (Gurtcheff et al., 2011) 4. Clinical studies have shown that gestagens, when used during lactation, do not adversely affect milk production or composition. (Kamal et al., 1969) 5. Long-term studies on children exposed to Depo-Provera during pregnancy or lactation indicate no significant adverse effects on growth or development. (Pardthaisong et al., 1992) 6. The use of long-acting contraceptive progestogens, such as Norplant, has been shown to have no detrimental effects on lactation. (Zanartu et al., 1976) 7. Subdermal contraceptive implants containing nomegestrol acetate, such as Uniplant, are safe for use during lactation and do not interfere with breastfeeding. (Abdel-Aleem et al., 1996) 8. Early postpartum use of Norplant implants does not alter maternal serum immunoglobulin levels or those of their breastfed infants. (Abdulla et al., 1985) 9. Norplant use during the postpartum period has been shown to be safe for both mothers and infants, with no significant adverse effects reported. (Affandi et al., 1986) 10. Progestogen-only contraceptives, such as desogestrel-containing pills, do not negatively impact breastfeeding or infant growth. (Baheiraei et al., 2001) 11. Comparative studies between progestogen-only pills and intrauterine contraceptive devices in lactating women have shown no significant differences in breastfeeding outcomes. (Bjarnadottir et al., 2001) 12. A single implant of elcometrine (ST-1435), a non-orally active progestin, has been demonstrated to be an effective long-acting contraceptive for postpartum nursing women. (Coutinho et al., 1999) 13. Progesterone implants, when compared to placebo and copper intrauterine devices, have been shown to be effective for fertility regulation in nursing women without adverse effects on lactation. (Croxatto et al., 1982) 14. Norplant levonorgestrel implants, when initiated early postpartum, do not interfere with lactation or infant growth. (Diaz et al., 1985) 15. Progesterone vaginal rings, progestin-only pills, Norplant implants, and Copper T 380-A intrauterine devices have been shown to have no significant adverse effects on lactation duration, infant growth, or bleeding patterns. (Diaz et al., 1997) 16. Continuous low-dose progestogen administration postpartum has been shown to maintain lactation effectively while serving as a contraceptive. (Zanartu et al., 1976) 17. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA), whether administered subcutaneously (DMPA-SC) or intramuscularly (DMPA-IM), has a similar safety profile, with no significant differences in weight changes, bleeding patterns, or bone mineral density. (WHO, 2023) 18. DMPA-SC is considered safe for use in women with medical conditions, including endometriosis, HIV, and obesity, with minimal adverse effects reported. (WHO, 2023) 19. DMPA-SC does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV, and the use of condoms is recommended for STI prevention. (WHO, 2023) 20. Women have the right to access evidence-based contraceptive information and make informed choices about their reproductive health. Contraceptive decisions are influenced by individual circumstances, societal, and cultural contexts. (WHO, 2023) 21. Studies have shown that DMPA-SC and DMPA-IM are therapeutically equivalent, with similar pharmacokinetics, contraceptive efficacy, and safety profiles. (WHO, 2023) 22. Evidence suggests that DMPA-SC is well-tolerated in women living with HIV, with rare occurrences of serious adverse events. (WHO, 2023) 23. Progestogen-only contraceptives, such as etonogestrel-releasing implants (Implanon), have been shown to have no adverse effects on breastfeeding or infant growth when compared to non-medicated intrauterine devices. (Reinprayoon et al., 2000) 24. Hormonal contraceptives, including levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems (Mirena), have been shown to be safe during lactation, with no significant impact on breastfeeding performance, infant growth, or development. (Shaamash et al., 2005) 25. The pharmacodynamic effects of levonorgestrel, whether administered orally or subdermally, do not adversely affect urinary hormone levels in breastfed male infants. (Shikary et al., 1986) 26. Hormonal contraceptives have been shown to have no significant impact on milk volume or infant growth, as demonstrated by the WHO Task Force on Oral Contraceptives. (Tankeyoon et al., 1984) 27. Progestogen-only contraceptives are generally well-accepted by breastfeeding women, with no significant adverse effects reported. (West, 1983) 28. Hormonal and non-hormonal contraceptives have been shown to have no significant impact on lactation or the incidence of pregnancy. (Zacharias et al., 1986) 29. Long-term follow-up studies of children breastfed by mothers using depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) have shown no adverse effects on growth or development. (Jimenez et al., 1976) 30. The use of hormonal contraceptives during lactation has been shown to have no significant impact on the initiation or maintenance of breastfeeding. (Kamal et al., 1970) 31. Nestorone implants have been shown to be effective and safe for postpartum women, with no significant adverse effects on lactation or infant health. (Massai et al., 2001) 32. Progestogen-only oral contraceptives have been shown to have no significant impact on breastfeeding or infant growth when compared to non-hormonal methods. (Moggia et al., 1991) 33. Etonogestrel-releasing implants (Implanon) have been shown to have no adverse effects on breastfeeding or infant growth when compared to intrauterine devices. (Taneepanichskul et al., 2006) 34. The use of hormonal contraceptives during lactation has been shown to have no significant impact on milk volume or infant growth. (Tankeyoon et al., 1984) 35. Women using DMPA-SC or DMPA-IM experience similar contraceptive efficacy, weight changes, and bleeding patterns, with no significant differences reported. (WHO, 2023) This detailed interpretation provides a professional and comprehensive understanding of the studies and findings related to contraceptive use during lactation.
